topic.name: Hydroxychloroquine
topic.short_description: Antimalarial drug studied for autophagy inhibition in cancer treatment
topic.seo_title: Hydroxychloroquine Cancer Research - Latest Studies & Findings | Your Cancer Breakthroughs
topic.seo_description: Explore Hydroxychloroquine cancer research. Learn how this antimalarial drug is being studied for autophagy inhibition in cancer treatment and latest clinical findings.
topic.seo_intro:
Hydroxychloroquine, traditionally known as an antimalarial medication, has emerged as a subject of significant interest in cancer research. Scientists are investigating how this drug may interrupt autophagy—a cellular process where cancer cells essentially recycle themselves to survive and proliferate. By potentially inhibiting autophagy, hydroxychloroquine could starve cancer cells of this critical survival mechanism, making it a promising candidate for off-label cancer treatment studies.

The research into hydroxychloroquine's anticancer potential represents an important example of drug repurposing in oncology. Rather than developing entirely new compounds, researchers are examining existing medications with established safety profiles to identify new therapeutic applications. This approach can accelerate the translation of scientific discoveries into clinical practice while potentially offering patients additional treatment options. Multiple clinical trials and laboratory studies are currently exploring hydroxychloroquine alone and in combination with conventional chemotherapy or targeted therapies across various cancer types.

On this page, you'll find the latest peer-reviewed research on hydroxychloroquine in cancer treatment. Our curated collection includes clinical trial results, mechanistic studies, and expert analysis to help patients, caregivers, and healthcare providers understand the current state of this research. While early findings are encouraging, it's important to note that hydroxychloroquine remains under investigation for cancer applications, and any use should only occur under direct medical supervision.

articles.title: Resveratrol synergizes with chloroquine to inhibit the malignant progression of oral squamous cell carcinoma by regulating KIF11.
articles.summary: Resveratrol and chloroquine together suppress oral squamous cell carcinoma growth by targeting the KIF11 protein.

articles.summary: Higher-dose hydroxychloroquine may benefit lupus patients more, but researchers need to weigh safety risks against these potential advantages.

articles.title: A Phase I Trial of MK-2206 and Hydroxychloroquine in Solid Tumors, Melanoma, Renal and Prostate Cancer to Examine the Role of Autophagy in Tumorigenesis
articles.summary: A trial testing whether combining two drugs—MK-2206 and hydroxychloroquine—kills advanced melanoma, prostate, and kidney cancer cells better than either drug alone.

articles.title: A phase I study of hydroxychloroquine and suba-itraconazole in men with biochemical relapse of prostate cancer (HITMAN-PC): dose escalation results.
articles.summary: Researchers tested a combination of two drugs to treat prostate cancer that has returned after initial treatment, establishing safe dosing levels.

articles.title: Hydroxychloroquine alleviates cyclophosphamide-induced premature ovarian failure by attenuating granulosa cell senescence and modulating the mtDNA-cGAS pathway.
articles.summary: Hydroxychloroquine protects ovaries from chemotherapy damage by reducing cell aging and inflammation in cancer patients receiving cyclophosphamide.

articles.title: Photocaged Chloroquine Derivatives for the Light-Dependent Inhibition of Autophagy in Cancer Stem Cells.
articles.summary: Researchers developed light-activated chloroquine drugs that kill cancer stem cells only when illuminated, reducing toxicity to healthy tissue.

articles.summary: In oral cancer, combining BET inhibitor JQ1 and autophagy inhibitor chloroquine enhances immunogenic cell death and antitumor immune response through nanoparticle delivery.

articles.title: Chloroquine phosphate targets the MAPK-ERK pathway to inhibit ASFV SY-1 replication in vitro.
articles.summary: Chloroquine phosphate inhibits African swine fever virus replication by blocking a key cellular signaling pathway called MAPK-ERK.
